name: Working Capital Timing
title: Working Capital Timing
answer: Working capital timing is the practice of managing when cash leaves and enters a business, chiefly through the gap between paying suppliers and collecting from customers. In an AI accounting context it covers the forecasting of that gap, the scheduling of payments and collections, and the measurement of how long cash stays tied up in the operating cycle. It sits alongside credit control and treasury rather than replacing them, and it draws on the same ledgers, invoices and bank feeds those functions already use.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Working capital timing is the practice of managing when cash leaves and enters a business, chiefly through the gap between paying suppliers and collecting from customers. In an AI accounting context it covers the forecasting of that gap, the scheduling of payments and collections, and the measurement of how long cash stays tied up in the operating cycle. It sits alongside credit control and treasury rather than replacing them, and it draws on the same ledgers, invoices and bank feeds those functions already use.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on the accounting system of record, typically an ERP or a cloud ledger, plus bank statement feeds and invoice data pulled from billing or procurement platforms. Forecasts are usually built in a spreadsheet or a planning tool, and increasingly in a dedicated cash forecasting module that reads directly from the ledger. Data quality is the binding constraint: unmatched invoices, late bank feeds and inconsistent payment terms will distort any timing model regardless of the software around it.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Analysts start from the receivables and payables ageing, then apply agreed payment terms, historical payment behaviour and known exceptions to project when each item will settle. Machine learning enters mainly as a prediction layer, estimating the actual payment date for a customer or the likely date a supplier will be paid, rather than assuming the contractual date. Those predictions feed a rolling cash position, which is then compared against obligations and revised as new invoices, disputes and receipts arrive. The output is a dated schedule of expected inflows and outflows, not a single balance.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Timing decisions touch contractual payment terms, supplier relationships and sometimes regulatory obligations on prompt payment, so the audit trail matters as much as the forecast. Teams need to show which data fed a projection, what assumptions were applied and who approved a change to a payment run. Where models predict customer payment behaviour, the inputs are often personal or commercially sensitive, which brings data protection and internal access controls into scope. The site tracks 229 compliance and regulation pages, reflecting how much of this area is shaped by rules rather than by modelling choice alone.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward continuous forecasting, where the cash position updates as transactions post rather than on a monthly close cycle. That shift depends less on new algorithms than on tighter integration between ledgers, banks and planning tools, and on cleaning up the payment terms data those systems rely on. Expect more emphasis on explainable predictions, since a treasurer has to justify holding or releasing cash, and on scenario testing for supplier delays or customer defaults. Adoption will likely track the general maturity of finance automation rather than move ahead of it.
